content: The laboratory should develop study plans, contracts, and detailed reports of its analyses. Participation in proficiency tests or collaborative trials is strongly recommended. The chosen laboratory must have robust infrastructure, including separate facilities for various activities such as sample receipt, preparation, chromatographic analysis, and storage of reagents and solvents, as well as appropriate workspaces and fume hoods. It should also be equipped with the necessary tools to conduct physico-chemical testing of pesticides in accordance with the methods of the Collaborative International Pesticides Analytical Council (CIPAC) and WHO specifications. Certified analytical standards, reagents, and solvents required for the analyses must be available. The laboratory must employ a sufficient number of qualified scientists and technicians. Regular training and participation in workshops on modern analytical techniques, such as gas chromatography and high-performance liquid chromatography, are recommended. Training in quality assurance is also advised. Access to WHO specifications, guidelines on pesticide analysis (available on the websites of FAO, WHO, OECD, and the European Union), and CIPAC and AOAC analytical methods is essential. Accreditation under ISO 17025 by a national body is generally more suitable for an official quality control laboratory than the quality assurance scheme under Good Laboratory Practice (GLP), which is mandatory for studies required for national registration in OECD countries. Guidelines for national laboratories on pesticide quality control provide general advice for establishing or strengthening such facilities, regardless of whether the products are used for public health or agriculture. While the intended use of a product may differ, the quality control schemes are similar, and a laboratory analyzing products for both areas can achieve synergy and optimize resource use. It also references laboratories involved in pre-registration testing of products. The guidelines extend beyond quality control for specific analyses to encompass the full range of laboratory management, including organization, staff procedures, and facilities. The WHO Collaborating Centre for Quality Control of Pesticides can be requested by procurement entities to perform quality control on procured pesticides. Proper sampling is critical for laboratory analysis. A well-documented sample should include sufficient pesticide quantities from a batch, copies of shipping and transaction records, and acknowledgment of receipt by the party from whom the samples are taken. Guidelines on sampling for quality control of technical-grade active ingredients and formulated products are detailed in the FAO and WHO specifications manual. For small-volume packages, three whole packages should be randomly selected from the same batch. For larger packages, subsampling is recommended to facilitate handling and minimize disposal issues. Subsamples should be thoroughly mixed and stored in appropriate containers to prevent contamination. Sampling procedures for specific products, such as long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) or mosquito coils, are outlined in the relevant guidelines. Samples must be properly labeled, sealed, and accompanied by a sampling report. They should be transported with care to avoid spillage or deterioration. Regulations for transporting hazardous materials, such as those by the International Civil Aviation Organization and International Maritime Organization, must be followed. Independent quality control laboratories should analyze the samples to verify compliance with WHO or other relevant specifications. A contract between the laboratory and the requesting party should outline all relevant details, including the tests to be performed, timelines, confidentiality clauses, and costs. The analysis should cover all physical and chemical properties specified in the WHO or other relevant specifications. Omission of critical tests may increase the risk of accepting substandard products and is not recommended. In exceptional cases, such as emergencies, some tests may be omitted with mutual agreement. The laboratory must provide a comprehensive report of the analysis, including detailed results, compliance conclusions, and any relevant information to aid interpretation. The report should be signed by the responsible analyst or laboratory manager and sent to the requesting party. National regulations for procurement typically include provisions for penalizing noncompliance with tender conditions. Bidders submitting incomplete or misleading offers may face disqualification, legal action, fines, or exclusion from future tenders. Customs clearance for pesticide imports requires familiarity with local procedures and collaboration with regulatory authorities. Emergency procurement provisions should allow for rapid acquisition of unregistered pesticides when necessary, with appropriate safeguards to prevent misuse. A traceability system should be in place to record the distribution of procured pesticides, ensuring they can be tracked to local warehouses. This system is essential for recalling noncompliant products and preventing unauthorized use.
